proof:
# Sharp dimensional weighted three-tail inequality

Let K be a full-dimensional convex body in R^d, let g be its volume
centroid, let u!=0, and normalize its directional cap function by

    F(s)=|K intersect {u.(x-g)>=s}|/|K|.

Set Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d and define

    lambda_1=1,
    lambda_d=[(2d/(d+1))^(d/(d-1))-1]^(d-1), d>=2.         (1)

Then for every real s,

    F(0)+F(s)+lambda_d F(-s)>=Gamma_d+lambda_d.             (2)

The coefficient lambda_d is the largest possible universal
coefficient in (2). In particular lambda_2=7/9. The constants
tend to4/e^2. This is an ordinary convex-body marginal theorem,
not a general mixed-integer depth assertion.

An equivalent useful sharp subset consequence is: for every
measurable E subset K, with a=|E| and V=|K|, every real t satisfies

    |K intersect {u.(x-g)>=0}|
      +|E intersect {u.(x-g)>=t}|
      +|K intersect {u.(x-g)>=-t}|
       >=Gamma_d V+lambda_d a.                            (3)

The three fibers E,K,K are actual convex-compatible fibers when
E is convex. Formula (3) keeps one normal and the opposite
thresholds of one actual cap; it cannot be summed over many pairs
while paying the middle term only once.

## 1. Constants and zero/negative shifts

Assume d>=2, and write Gamma=Gamma_d, lambda=lambda_d,
p=d-1, a0=d/(d+1), and k=lambda^(1/p). Definition (1) gives

    (1+k)^p=(2a0)^d=2^d Gamma.                            (4)

There is a convenient uniform upper bound

    0<lambda<=4Gamma^2<1.                                (5)

Indeed, for L=4Gamma^2, arithmetic-geometric mean gives
(1+L^(1/p))^p>=2^p sqrt(L)=2^d Gamma. Comparing with (4)
and using monotonicity in L proves (5). It also gives

    lambda<=Gamma/(1-Gamma),

because 4Gamma(1-Gamma)<=1. Thus at s=0, ordinary Grunbaum gives
(2+lambda)F(0)>=(2+lambda)Gamma>=Gamma+lambda.

For s<0, the left side of (2) is at least its value at -s,
since lambda<=1 and F is nonincreasing. It suffices to treat s>0.
For d=1 the law is a centered uniform interval: F(0)=1/2 and
F(s)+F(-s)=1 for every s, proving (2) with lambda_1=1.

## 2. Dirac-safe ordinary localization

For d>=2 the centered scalar marginal is nonatomic and is a
1/d-concave probability measure. In terms of its CDF G, (2) for
s>0 is equivalent to

    G(0)+G(s)+lambda G(-s)<=2-Gamma.                       (6)

If this were strictly violated, nonatomicity would preserve a
strict violation after replacing G(0) by G(-epsilon), for some
0<epsilon<s. On a fixed compact interval containing the support,
apply the same one-constraint localization theorem already used
and independently audited in
`candidate dafd411c026c302c`,
Section1, and `candidate 732b11a769399016`,
Section2. The constraint is integral x dnu>=0, and the affine
upper-semicontinuous objective is

    nu{x<=-epsilon}+nu{x<=s}+lambda nu{x<=-s}.

Every admissible Dirac lies at a nonnegative point and has objective
at most1<2-Gamma. The non-Dirac extremizers have mean zero and
density proportional to a nonnegative affine function to the
power d-1 on an interval. Their regularized objective is no larger
than their unregularized objective. Thus it suffices to prove (2)
for both orientations of every such affine-power law.

This invocation retains the existing primary one-constraint
localization input (Fradelizi--Guedon, Theorem2), with parameter
1/d<=1/2. It makes no new localization assertion, and does not
pass an unshifted discontinuous central CDF through a Dirac limit.

## 3. Scalar notation and two elementary mean bounds

Every nonconstant affine-power law can be written, before
centering and possibly reflecting, as

    f(x)=d x^(d-1)/(1-r^d), r<=x<=1, 0<=r<1,
    G(x)=(x^d-r^d)/(1-r^d) on its support, clipped outside.

Its mean, central CDF and paired inner CDF are

    m=a0(1-r^(d+1))/(1-r^d),
    p0=G(m), c=2m-1, T=G(c).                              (7)

Here m>=(1+r)/2, hence c>=r. Also

    Gamma<=p0<=1/2.                                      (8)

For completeness set R=r^d, alpha=1/d, and

    m(R)=integral_0^1 [R+(1-R)v]^alpha dv, g(R)=m(R)^d.

The function g is concave on [0,1]. On (0,1), if I,A,B denote
the integrals of h^alpha, h^(alpha-1)(1-v),
h^(alpha-2)(1-v)^2 respectively, with h=R+(1-R)v, then

    g''=(1-alpha) I^(1/alpha-2)(A^2-I B)<=0

by Cauchy--Schwarz. Its endpoints are g(0)=Gamma and g(1)=1,
so g(R)>=Gamma+(1-Gamma)R. This gives the lower bound in (8).
Jensen gives m(R)<=((1+R)/2)^alpha, so g(R)<=(1+R)/2 and
therefore p0<=1/2. The midpoint lower bound for m follows by
pairing the increasing density about the interval midpoint.

## 4. The decreasing orientation, with the sharp constant

For the reflected law, F(s)=G(m-s). The expression in (2) is

    p0+J(s),  J(s)=G(m-s)+lambda G(m+s).

On 0<=s<=1-m, both arguments are in the support and
J'=-f(m-s)+lambda f(m+s). Its unique critical minimum is at

    s_*=m(1-k)/(1+k),

if that point belongs to this interval. After s=1-m, the upper
CDF is one and J decreases to its final constant lambda.
Consequently the global minimum is either lambda or J(s_*),
the latter only when m<=(1+k)/2. The constant branch is handled
by p0>=Gamma.

For the critical branch put A=2^d lambda/(1+k)^(d-1)=lambda/Gamma.
Direct substitution gives

    p0+J(s_*)=[(1+A)g(R)-(2+lambda)R]/(1-R).              (9)

The mean increases strictly from a0 to1. The threshold (1+k)/2
lies strictly between them: it is a0(2a0)^(1/(d-1))>a0,
and k<1 by (5). There is a unique R_* with m(R_*)=(1+k)/2.
Define the concave function

    H(R)=(1+A)g(R)-(Gamma+lambda)-(2-Gamma)R.

At R=0 its value is A Gamma-lambda=0. At R=R_* the critical
upper threshold equals1 and (9) becomes
p0+G(2m-1)+lambda>=Gamma+lambda. Hence H(R_*)>=0.
Concavity proves H>=0 throughout [0,R_*], exactly the critical
branch required by (9). This proves the decreasing orientation
for every d>=2, without assuming that untruncated cones minimize
all intermediate scalar expressions.

## 5. The increasing orientation in dimensions two through six

For the original increasing law the expression in (2) is

    1-p0+1-G(m+s)+lambda[1-G(m-s)].

It decreases up to s=1-m because f is increasing and lambda<=1.
Afterwards it is nondecreasing. Its minimum is

    1-p0+lambda(1-T).

We must prove

    p0+lambda T<=1-Gamma.                                (10)

This paragraph supplies a finite exact polynomial certificate for
the low dimensions. Put

    U=d sum_(i=0)^d r^i, W=(d+1) sum_(i=0)^(d-1) r^i,
    P_d,l(r)=[1-Gamma+(Gamma+l)r^d] W^d
                         -U^d-l(2U-W)^d.                (11)

Then P_d,l divided by (1-r^d)W^d is exactly
1-Gamma-p0-lT. All denominators are positive for 0<=r<1.

For d=2 take l=lambda_2=7/9. Direct division gives

    P_2,7/9(r)/(1-r)=(2+6r-21r^2+49r^3)/9.               (12)

Its numerator starts at2 and has derivative
147(r-1/7)^2+3>0, so it is positive throughout [0,1].

For d=3,4,5,6 we prove the stronger statement with l=1, which
implies (10) by (5). Let Q_d=P_d,1/(1-r), a polynomial of degree
d^2-1. Write Q_d=sum_(k=0)^N c_k r^k. Its coefficients in the
Bernstein basis binom(N,i)r^i(1-r)^(N-i) are exactly

    b_i=sum_(k=0)^i c_k binom(i,k)/binom(N,k).             (13)

All these coefficients are strictly positive. Here is a compact
exact summary of the arithmetic certificate:

| d | N | minimum Bernstein coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 8 | 2 |
| 4 | 15 | 32 |
| 5 | 24 | 502 |
| 6 | 35 | 8712 |

Here are the full coefficient certificates, listed in increasing
index order. The Bernstein coefficient vector for d=3 is 1/70 times

    [140,210,330,465,531,450,405,2835,28350].

For d=4 it is 1/9009 times

    [288288,384384,521664,722304,1015773,1439568,2038392,
     2860592,3950408,5339808,7079232,9518784,14783472,
     33551232,116468352,521224704].

For d=5 it is 1/178474296 times

    [89594096592,111992620740,141208087020,179719383480,
     231067778760,300303989622,394621080750,524249216400,
     703717669200,953628776100,1303138575375,1793399858250,
     2482300507500,3450962926125,4812850428750,6727712696250,
     9427739230000,13281714355000,18987532687500,
     28208619562500,45765058462500,87382082287500,
     208058350500000,612111062062500,2127748247625000].

In dimension6 an even simpler certificate is that ALL MONOMIAL
coefficients c_k themselves are positive. Their complete vector is

    [8712,60984,243936,731808,1829520,4024944,7656985,
     12704407,18695404,24737916,29670690,32335086,31587318,
     27626130,22586067,20396341,25905292,43270444,73801371,
     117665373,171895962,229957278,282864435,321859797,
     339523604,335492948,310913099,269765181,218594358,
     164638530,113891946,73425534,43146348,22397732,
     9627401,2868335].

Each displayed vector is the exact expansion of (11)--(13); the
standard-library verifier independently reconstructs it using
rational polynomial arithmetic. The vectors are also saved as
structured data in `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/sharp_weighted_three_tails_bernstein_certificates.json`.
All entries are strictly positive. Nonnegativity of the Bernstein
basis functions for d=3,4,5, and of monomials for d=6, proves
Q_d>0 on [0,1] without any approximate root or sign test. This
completes (10) for d<=6.

## 6. The increasing orientation in every dimension at least seven

We use the already proved quadrature inequality from
`candidate 732b11a769399016`, Section5
equation(10): for 0<alpha<1 and 0<=R<1,

    [2/(1-R)] integral_R^1 v^alpha dv
        <=1+[(1+5R)/6]^alpha.

That archived proof is an exact positive Stieltjes-integral argument,
based on an explicitly differentiated logarithmic inequality. It
is not a numerical bound and is not the isolated d=3 estimate5/32.
Applying it with alpha=1/d and R=r^d gives

    2m-1<=((1+5R)/6)^(1/d),
    T=[(2m-1)^d-R]/(1-R)<=1/6.                           (14)

The latter is also the archived Section6 equation(13).

The sequence Gamma_d decreases: differentiation of
-d log(1+1/d), together with log(1+x)>x/(1+x), proves this.
For every d>=7, equations (5), (8) and (14) therefore imply

    p0+lambda T<=1/2+(2/3)Gamma_d^2<=1-Gamma_d,

because the function x+(2/3)x^2 is increasing for x>=0 and
the following exact positive gap holds at Gamma_7=(7/8)^7:

    1/2-Gamma_7-(2/3)Gamma_7^2
       =29669536175/6597069766656>0.                     (15)

This proves (10) in all remaining dimensions. Constant affine
densities are uniform interval laws, whose expression is at least
1/2+lambda>=Gamma+lambda. Localization now completes (2).

## 7. Sharpness of the coefficient

Take the scalar cone law with G(x)=x^d on [0,1], mean a0=d/(d+1),
and the decreasing orientation F(s)=G(a0-s). This is realized by
a facet-normal marginal of an ordinary simplex. Put

    v=(2a0)^(-1/(d-1)), s_*=v-a0>0.

The strict positivity of s_* follows from 2Gamma<1. Also v<1,
and 2a0-v>0, so both cuts are proper. Equation (4) gives
v^d=1/(1+k) and 2a0-v=kv. Therefore

    F(0)=Gamma,
    F(s_*)=k^d/(1+k),
    1-F(-s_*)=k/(1+k),
    F(s_*)/[1-F(-s_*)]=k^(d-1)=lambda.

Equality holds in (2), and any larger coefficient fails at this
same actual simplex marginal and shift. For d=1 the centered
interval proves sharpness of lambda_1=1 directly.

Writing p=d-1, expansion of the elementary expression (1) gives
k=1+(2 log2-2)/p+O(p^-2); hence lambda_d tends to4/e^2.
The coefficient is greater than1/2: this is equivalent to the
elementary constant inequality already proved in Section5 of
`candidate dafd411c026c302c`.
No monotonicity of lambda_d is needed or asserted here.

## 8. The sharp measurable-subset payment

Restore unnormalized cap volumes. For E subset K,

    |E intersect {u.(x-g)>=t}|>=max(0,a-V+F(t)).

After subtracting lambda a from the proposed total in (3), the
right side furnished by this bound is nonincreasing up to a=V-F(t)
and nondecreasing afterwards, since 0<lambda<=1. Its minimum is

    F(0)+F(-t)+lambda F(t)-lambda V>=Gamma V

by (2), applied with s=-t. This proves (3) for every measurable
subset, with null-boundary conventions inherited from K.

The coefficient is sharp here too. In the simplex equality example
from Section7, take t=-s_* and E=K intersect {u.(x-g)<=-s_*}.
Then a=V[1-F(-s_*)]>0, the E-cap at threshold t has zero volume,
and the other two terms give exactly Gamma V+lambda a. This E is
an actual convex cap subbody, so its three fibers E,K,K are
convex-compatible and the equality does not require a fractional
source or a nonconvex subset.
